opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really good question, because there's a very natural cynical view that says history is just interests all the way down: people who have power use it to keep power, and moral arguments are mostly window dressing that gets wheeled out after the fact to justify whatever the winners were going to do anyway.

I don't think that view is crazy. Interests matter enormously, and a lot of moral talk *is* rationalization. But when you look at some of the most striking changes in moral history, the purely interest-based story struggles to explain them. Take the abolition of the slave trade in Britain. It was enormously profitable, and the people who benefited were well represented in Parliament. Yet a campaign that was explicitly moral, built on pamphlets, testimony, boycotts of slave-grown sugar, and arguments about the common humanity of enslaved people, managed to turn the country against it, at real economic cost. You can tell clever stories about hidden economic motives, but historians have found those stories pretty unconvincing.

So part of my answer is that moral reasoning works through a slightly indirect channel. It doesn't usually persuade the powerful to give up their power directly. What it does is change what large numbers of people regard as legitimate. Once enough people come to see a practice as indefensible, the cost of defending it rises. Politicians face different voters, businesses face different customers, and the people inside the institutions start to feel uncomfortable. The argument doesn't need to defeat self-interest head-on; it reshapes the landscape that self-interest operates in.

There's also something about consistency. People really do care about not being hypocrites, at least publicly. If you hold up a principle that a society already professes, "all men are created equal," say, and show that current practice contradicts it, you've got real leverage. Much of moral progress has been extending principles people already accepted to groups they'd previously excluded. That's moral reasoning doing genuine work.

And I think this matters a lot for how we think about the future. If you believe change is only ever driven by power, you'll be fairly fatalistic about things like concern for future generations, who have no votes and no money and literally can't lobby us. But if moral reasoning can expand the circle of concern, as it has before, then there's real hope that we can come to take seriously the interests of people who don't yet exist, and that we'll act to protect humanity's long-term potential even though nobody alive today is paid to do so. That, to me, is one of the main reasons it's worth making these arguments carefully and publicly.

r001.rationale: The response gives British abolition as an example of moral reasoning driving change, but does not identify belief in the moral rightness of extending voting rights as a key cause of women gaining suffrage in England.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the puzzle you're pointing at is real, and it's worth taking seriously. If you look at history through a purely cynical lens, you'd expect the people with power to simply keep it, and you'd expect moral argument to be a kind of decoration on top of what was going to happen anyway. But I don't think that's what the historical record actually shows.

Take the abolition of the slave trade. The people who benefited from slavery had enormous incentives to preserve it, and they were extremely well represented in Parliament. And yet Britain abolished the trade, and then went further and spent something like two percent of its national income for decades suppressing it, with the Royal Navy patrolling the Atlantic. That's not what you'd predict if power and self-interest were the whole story. What you see instead is a sustained moral campaign, with pamphlets and petitions and arguments, gradually changing what people thought was acceptable, until the political equilibrium shifted underneath the people who were defending the status quo.

And I think the mechanism matters here. Moral reasoning doesn't work by persuading the king to give up his throne. It works on the much larger number of people who aren't directly invested, who have some latent sense that something is wrong, and who can be moved by a clear argument that makes that discomfort explicit. Once enough of those people change their minds, the incentives of the powerful change too, because preserving power now requires accommodating the new consensus rather than fighting it.

The other thing I'd say is that people with power are also moral agents. They aren't purely calculating machines. They have children, they care about how they'll be remembered, they're embedded in communities that have standards. So even for them, an argument that something is unjust isn't inert. It raises the psychological cost of continuing, and it removes the comfortable rationalisations that let people do things they'd otherwise be ashamed of.

So I'd put it this way: incentives explain a lot of what happens in the short run, but over longer time scales, ideas about what's right and wrong seem to be one of the most important forces shaping where societies end up. The expansion of the moral circle, from the tribe to the nation to all of humanity and increasingly to animals and future generations, is hard to explain without giving moral reasoning a real causal role. That doesn't mean it's fast or reliable. But it does mean that if you want to change the world, getting the arguments right and making them well is not a naive strategy. It's one of the few that has a track record.

r001.rationale: The response discusses moral reasoning as a cause of social change and gives abolition as an example, but it does not identify the belief that extending voting rights was morally right as a key cause of women gaining suffrage in England.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a temptation to look at social change and assume that the real explanation must always be about interests or power, and that moral arguments are just a kind of decoration. But that leaves something important unexplained: people sometimes come to believe that arrangements which benefit them are wrong, and then work to change them.

That doesn’t mean moral reasoning operates independently of incentives. Often it’s up against very strong incentives. But it can expose a tension between things people already believe. If you think that everyone deserves some basic consideration, and then someone points out that you’re excluding a whole group without a defensible reason, you have a problem. You can resist the argument, of course. But you can also change your mind, and sometimes that changes what you’re willing to do.

And the argument doesn’t have to persuade everyone who holds power. It can persuade other people to organise, to challenge an institution, or to bear costs they wouldn’t otherwise have borne. That can change the incentives facing the people in power.

So I wouldn’t say moral reasoning is the whole explanation of social progress. But I think we miss a major part of the explanation if we treat people’s moral convictions as merely a disguise for what benefits them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses moral convictions as a general force for social change, but does not identify the belief that extending voting rights was morally right as a key cause of women gaining suffrage in England.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s a temptation to see moral arguments as just a kind of window dressing for people’s interests. And of course people do use them that way. But that doesn’t mean that moral reasoning has no independent force.

One striking thing about moral arguments is that they can have implications their proponents would rather avoid. You might defend your own freedom by appealing to a general principle about the importance of liberty. But then someone else can ask, “Why doesn’t that apply to us?” And you have to either find a morally relevant difference, abandon the principle, or accept that their freedom matters too.

That doesn’t automatically overcome material interests. It can take a great deal of organising and struggle. But it gives people a way to challenge the legitimacy of existing power, and it can persuade people who benefit from that power to support change.

So I wouldn’t say moral reasoning is the whole explanation of social progress. But I think an account that treats every moral argument as merely a disguise for self-interest misses something important: people can recognise an inconsistency in their beliefs, feel the force of it, and change what they’re willing to defend.
